_readme: Verified survivors a month's editor did not use, each tagged with the month it fits, routed forward rather than thrown away. The Makers' carry delivered 29 pre-verified entries by December. Appended by land-month.js from month.json's `unused`; read by prep-month.js into the next month's brief. Never edited by hand.

entries.quote: Listen to the reed how it tells a tale, complaining of separations.
entries.source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, line 1 (trans. Reynold A. Nicholson, 1926)
entries.note: Verified opening line. Nicholson later revised it after the oldest manuscript to Listen to this reed how it complains; the 1926 wording ships with the 1926 date. Held for a quieter month.

entries.quote: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, ch. 1, ‘An Unexpected Party’, first sentence
entries.note: Verified opening line, pure delight; January had more openings than days. Mind the cap: the Calendar For Life bank carries many Tolkien lines.

entries.quote: I am large, I contain multitudes.
entries.source: Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass, ‘Song of Myself’, section 51, 1881 text
entries.note: Verified; parenthetical in the source. Not a beginning line so much as a truth-and-clarity line.

entries.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
entries.source: Italo Calvino, Why Read the Classics?, definition 6 (trans. Patrick Creagh, 1986)
entries.note: Verified. Calvino appears in January with the opening of If on a winter’s night a traveler; one person per month.

entries.quote: Our battered suitcases were piled on the sidewalk again; we had longer ways to go. But no matter, the road is life.
entries.source: Jack Kerouac, On the Road, Part Three, ch. 5, closing sentence (Sal Paradise)
entries.note: Verified against fifteen scans of the Viking and Penguin text; it closes chapter 5 of Part Three. A road line, for the month of the Way.

entries.quote: And, when you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
entries.source: Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist, Part One (Melchizedek, the king of Salem) (trans. Alan R. Clarke, 1993)
entries.note: Verified in Clarke’s translation with the leading And; Melchizedek speaks it. Hope rather than beginning.

entries.quote: yes I said yes I will Yes.
entries.source: James Joyce, Ulysses, episode 18, Penelope, closing words (Molly Bloom)
entries.note: Verified closing words of the novel, lowercase because the sentence runs on. Bloomsday is 16 June.

entries.quote: Light, my light, the world-filling light, the eye-kissing light, heart-sweetening light!
entries.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 57, first line (trans. the author, 1912)
entries.note: Verified in Tagore’s own English of 1912. A light line for the dark month.

entries.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, ch. 1 (1929)
entries.note: Verified. Woolf’s other survivor, the opening of Mrs Dalloway, is the stronger January line, and neither made the month; one person per month either way.

entries.quote: But man is not made for defeat. A man can be destroyed but not defeated.
entries.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea, unchaptered, after the first shark (Santiago) (Scribner, 1952)
entries.note: Verified in the 1952 Scribner text; Santiago says it aloud. A courage line.

entries.quote: Barrabás came to us by sea, the child Clara wrote in her delicate calligraphy.
entries.source: Isabel Allende, The House of the Spirits, chapter 1, the opening sentence (trans. Magda Bogin, 1985)
entries.note: Verified opening line in Bogin’s translation; it returns as the novel’s last line. Held for a month that can use a pure opening.

entries.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway, the opening sentence (1925)
entries.note: Verified opening line. Held because January had more openings than days.

entries.quote: Ships at a distance have every man’s wish on board.
entries.source: Zora Neale Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God, chapter 1, the opening sentence (1937)
entries.note: Verified opening line. The paragraph goes on to say some ships never land, so it is hopeful only as a single sentence; place it with that in mind.

entries.quote: We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
entries.source: Joan Didion, The White Album, the title essay, opening sentence (Simon and Schuster, 1979)
entries.note: Verified opening line. The essay goes on to test the claim, so the line is cooler than it reads alone; a truth-and-clarity line.

entries.quote: This book was written in good faith, reader.
entries.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, To the Reader, the opening sentence (trans. Donald M. Frame, 1957)
entries.note: Verified opening line in Frame’s rendering. Good faith belongs with plain speech.

entries.quote: And it seemed as though in a little while the solution would be found, and then a new and splendid life would begin; and it was clear to both of them that they had still a long, long road before them, and that the most complicated and difficult part of it was only just beginning.
entries.source: Anton Chekhov, The Lady with the Dog, section IV, the closing sentence (trans. Constance Garnett, 1917)
entries.note: Verified closing line. Chekhov appears in January with Trofimov’s Welcome to the new life; one person per month.

entries.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
entries.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 1, 980a21 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
entries.note: Verified opening line of the Metaphysics in Ross. Held because January had more openings than days.

entries.quote: Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.
entries.source: Plotinus, Enneads, I.6.9, On Beauty (trans. Stephen MacKenna, 1917)
entries.note: Verified in MacKenna 1917. A clarity line rather than a beginning line.

entries.quote: If it were customary to send daughters to school like sons, and if they were then taught the natural sciences, they would learn as thoroughly and understand the subtleties of all the arts and sciences as well as sons.
entries.source: Christine de Pizan, The Book of the City of Ladies, Part I, ch. 27, p. 63 (Lady Reason) (trans. Earl Jeffrey Richards, 1982)
entries.note: Corrected to Richards 1982; the little girls wording is Rosalind Brown-Grant, Penguin 1999. Page 63 is the 1982 Persea printing; the 1998 reissue paginates differently. Lady Reason speaks. A justice line.

entries.quote: Had Aristotle prepared victuals, he would have written more.
entries.source: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Reply to Sor Filotea de la Cruz, the philosophies of the kitchen (trans. Margaret Sayers Peden, 1982)
entries.note: Corrected: trimmed to the sentence confirmed in Peden’s translation; the lead-in clause about trivial details was not checked. The refuter confirmed the wording in the Penguin 1997 reprint, p. 43, which the citation may name instead.

entries.quote: Tell me about a complicated man.
entries.source: Homer, The Odyssey, Book 1, line 1 (trans. Emily Wilson, 2017)
entries.note: Verified opening line of Wilson’s Odyssey. Held because January had more openings than days; a line for hard roads.

entries.quote: Although the wind blows terribly here, the moonlight also leaks between the roof planks of this ruined house.
entries.source: Izumi Shikibu, ‘Although the wind’, The Ink Dark Moon (trans. Jane Hirshfield with Mariko Aratani, 1988)
entries.note: Verified in Hirshfield and Aratani. A stillness line.

entries.quote: No coward soul is mine, no trembler in the world’s storm-troubled sphere: I see Heaven’s glories shine, and faith shines equal, arming me from fear.
entries.source: Emily Brontë, No Coward Soul Is Mine, lines 1 to 4, Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey, with Literary Remains of Ellis Bell (1850)
entries.note: Verified in the 1850 text as reprinted in 1908. A courage line.

entries.quote: Yes, of course it hurts when buds are breaking. Why else would the springtime falter?
entries.source: Karin Boye, Yes, Of Course It Hurts, lines 1 and 2, För trädets skull (1935) (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
entries.note: Verified in McDuff. Buds breaking: a spring line.

entries.quote: Another heavenly day.
entries.source: Samuel Beckett, Happy Days, Act I, Winnie’s first words after the bell (Grove Press, 1961) (Winnie)
entries.note: Verified opening line, but it is the ironic optimism of a woman buried to the waist, and a VERIFIED line may carry no note. Place it only where the source line can carry the context.

entries.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things can not be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one’s lifetime.
entries.source: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, Conclusion (American Publishing Company, 1869)
entries.note: Verified in the 1869 first edition, p. 650; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 1. A road line more than a kindness line.

entries.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
entries.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
entries.note: CORRECTED: the sentence is in The Return, Part II, not The Scot Abroad. The real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 36. A road line.

entries.quote: Surround yourself with human beings, my dear James. They are easier to fight for than principles.
entries.source: Ian Fleming, Casino Royale, chapter 20, The Nature of Evil (Jonathan Cape, 1953) (René Mathis)
entries.note: Verified in the chapter text; people over abstractions, spoken by Mathis. A service line.

entries.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
entries.note: Verified with the two-word for ever; the Calendar For Life copy modernised it. Only one Tolkien may land in a month and the bank carries many.

entries.quote: If more of us valued food and cheer and song above hoarded gold, it would be a merrier world.
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, chapter 18, The Return Journey (George Allen and Unwin, 1937) (Thorin Oakenshield)
entries.note: Verified in Thorin’s farewell; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 511. A gratitude line.

entries.quote: I rebel—therefore we exist.
entries.source: Albert Camus, The Rebel, Part One, The Rebel (trans. Anthony Bower, 1953)
entries.note: Verified in Bower with his em dash, the last sentence of Part One; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 3. Camus stands at one for the year.

entries.quote: There is no religion without love, and people may talk as much as they like about their religion, but if it does not teach them to be good and kind to man and beast it is all a sham.
entries.source: Anna Sewell, Black Beauty, Part I, chapter 13 (John Manly)
entries.note: CORRECTED: Sewell’s sentence runs on, all a sham, James, and it won’t stand when things come to be turned inside out; the line is cut at the clause and given a full stop, and the first word is raised to a capital.

entries.quote: As far as the education of children is concerned I think they should be taught not the little virtues but the great ones. Not thrift but generosity and an indifference to money; not caution but courage and a contempt for danger; nor shrewdness but frankness and a love of truth; not tact but love for one’s neighbour and self-denial; not a desire for success but a desire to be and to know.
entries.source: Natalia Ginzburg, The Little Virtues, title essay, 1960, opening sentences (trans. Dick Davis, 1985)
entries.note: CORRECTED to the book’s nor shrewdness; the anthologies smooth it to not, and PN Review 44 (1985) printed Davis with not and a differently worded first sentence. A counsel line.

entries.quote: Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business.
entries.source: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol, Stave One (Jacob Marley’s Ghost)
entries.note: Verified in Stave One with the first-edition commas. A December line by its book.

entries.quote: Let the tears of the poor man find with thee more compassion, but not more justice, than the pleadings of the rich.
entries.source: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, chapter 42 (Don Quixote, to Sancho Panza) (trans. John Ormsby, 1885)
entries.note: Verified in Ormsby. Compassion tempered by justice: a September line.

entries.quote: If a man should importune me to give a reason why I loved him, I find it could no otherwise be expressed, than by making answer: because it was he, because it was I.
entries.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book I, chapter 27, Of Friendship (trans. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877)
entries.note: Verified in Cotton and Hazlitt, whose numbering is 27 (28 in Villey). January routed Montaigne’s good faith to June; one Montaigne per month.

entries.quote: You become responsible, forever, for what you have tamed.
entries.source: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, The Little Prince, chapter XXI (the fox) (trans. Katherine Woods, 1943)
entries.note: Verified in Woods, the fox’s own line. A responsibility line.

entries.quote: It is justice, not charity, that is wanting in the world!
entries.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4 (1792)
entries.note: Verified in the 1792 text. Reads as the corrective to a compassion month, and is the September line itself. January routed a different Wollstonecraft line to March.

entries.quote: The good we secure for ourselves is precarious and uncertain, is floating in mid-air, until it is secured for all of us and incorporated into our common life.
entries.source: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House, Chapter VI, The Subjective Necessity for Social Settlements (Macmillan, 1910)
entries.note: Verified in the 1910 text and the 1893 Crowell printing of the paper; a lifted final clause with its first letter raised, every word in order.

entries.quote: The greatest benefit we owe to the artist, whether painter, poet, or novelist, is the extension of our sympathies.
entries.source: George Eliot, The Natural History of German Life, Westminster Review, July 1856; in Essays of George Eliot, ed. Sheppard (1883), essay V
entries.note: Verified twice in the Sheppard edition; refuted only as a month collision with the Middlemarch line, which landed. Eliot stands at two for the year after February.

entries.quote: To will oneself free is also to will others free.
entries.source: Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity, Part II, Personal Freedom and Others (trans. Bernard Frechtman, 1948)
entries.note: Verified in Frechtman. Beauvoir stands at one for the year.

entries.quote: Forgiving, in other words, is the only reaction which does not merely re-act but acts anew and unexpectedly, unconditioned by the act which provoked it and therefore freeing from its consequences both the one who forgives and the one who is forgiven.
entries.source: Hannah Arendt, The Human Condition, chapter V, section 33, Irreversibility and the Power to Forgive (Chicago, 1958), p. 241
entries.note: Verified against the Chicago text. Arendt stands at one for the year; forgiveness as beginning anew is a December line.

entries.quote: How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it.
entries.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, Section I, Chapter I, Of Sympathy (6th edition, 1790)
entries.note: Verified: the opening sentence of the book in the 6th edition.

entries.quote: Yet minds are not conquered by force, but by love and high-mindedness.
entries.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Appendix, XI (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
entries.note: Verified in Elwes. January routed Spinoza’s closing sentence to March; one Spinoza per month.

entries.quote: The good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.
entries.source: Bertrand Russell, What I Believe, chapter II, The Good Life (E. P. Dutton, 1925), p. 20
entries.note: Verified in the 1925 Dutton text, italicised as his creed. A counsel line.

entries.quote: You must sit down, sayes Love, and taste my meat: / So I did sit and eat.
entries.source: George Herbert, Love (III), lines 17 to 18, The Temple (Cambridge, 1633)
entries.note: Verified in two copies of the 1633 printing, closing couplet of the last poem of The Church. A gratitude line.

entries.quote: For there is no friend like a sister / In calm or stormy weather; / To cheer one on the tedious way, / To fetch one if one goes astray, / To lift one if one totters down, / To strengthen whilst one stands.
entries.source: Christina Rossetti, Goblin Market, lines 562 to 567, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862) (Laura)
entries.note: Verified, the closing lines of the poem. Lifting one who totters is a trial line.

entries.quote: Here is thy footstool and there rest thy feet where live the poorest, and lowliest, and lost.
entries.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 10, opening sentence (the author’s own English, 1912)
entries.note: Verified in the Macmillan text; a prose poem, so no line breaks. January routed Light, my light to December; one Tagore per month.

entries.quote: My heart is moved by all I cannot save: / so much has been destroyed / I have to cast my lot with those / who age after age, perversely, / with no extraordinary power, / reconstitute the world.
entries.source: Adrienne Rich, Natural Resources, closing six lines, The Dream of a Common Language (W. W. Norton, 1978)
entries.note: Verified against three postings crediting the 1978 edition; the Norton page itself was not opened. A trial line.

entries.quote: Somebody loves us all.
entries.source: Elizabeth Bishop, Filling Station, closing line, Questions of Travel (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1965)
entries.note: Verified, the closing line of the poem; four words, a very bare card. A gratitude line.

entries.quote: You do not have to be good. / You do not have to walk on your knees / for a hundred miles through the desert repenting. / You only have to let the soft animal of your body / love what it loves.
entries.source: Mary Oliver, Wild Geese, lines 1 to 5, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986), p. 14
entries.note: Verified against reprints crediting Dream Work, no comma before repenting; later printings add one. A renewal line.

entries.quote: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
entries.source: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet, 13 April 1942 (trans. Raymond Rosenthal, 1976, in Pétrement, Simone Weil: A Life, p. 462)
entries.note: Carried from January and held again: February took Weil’s What are you going through?, verified on the page, and one Weil per month. Page 462 rests on four scholarly citations. An attention line.

entries.quote: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
entries.source: Sappho, If Not, Winter, Fragment 16, lines 1 to 4 (trans. Anne Carson, 2002)
entries.note: Carried from January, verified in Carson, p. 27. Before it lands, the four lines must be marked with slashes in Carson’s lineation, which nobody has yet checked against the page; it is carried as prose.

entries.quote: A thousand words leave not the same / Deep print as does a single deed.
entries.source: Henrik Ibsen, Brand, Act II (The Man) (trans. F. E. Garrett, 1894)
entries.note: Verified in Garrett’s verse, p. 51 of the Everyman reprint. Ibsen landed in March with Nora’s line; one person per month. The deed over the word: a service line.

entries.quote: Our life is March weather, savage and serene in one hour.
entries.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Representative Men, IV, Montaigne; or, the Skeptic (Phillips, Sampson and Company, 1850), p. 174
entries.note: Verified in the 1850 first edition, p. 174. It says March but is about moods and the inconstancy of belief, not discipline; the refuter named it the first to drop. Spring weather, for April.

entries.quote: The maturity of man—that means, to have reacquired the seriousness that one had as a child at play.
entries.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, chapter IV, Apophthegms and Interludes, section 94 (trans. Helen Zimmern, 1907)
entries.note: CORRECTED: Zimmern’s translation is 1907, not 1906. The real text behind the Calendar For Life card that travels as Heraclitus; it is Nietzsche’s. Nietzsche landed in March with section 188; after March he stands at two of three.

entries.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
entries.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book II, chapter 14 (Jake Barnes) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926)
entries.note: Verified in the Scribner 1926 text via Project Gutenberg 67138; no page claimed. One Hemingway per month, and 03-cfl-12 is the other.

entries.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
entries.source: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, plate 7 (c. 1790 to 1793)
entries.note: Verified, the tenth Proverb of Hell, plate 7. Time and what is made in it: an impermanence line more than a discipline line.

entries.quote: He who reads much and travels much sees and knows a great deal.
entries.source: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, chapter 25 (Don Quixote) (trans. John Ormsby, 1885)
entries.note: Verified in Ormsby; the capital H is the card’s, since the clause follows Now I declare. Don Quixote says it in wonder at Master Pedro’s fraudulent ape, so a note on where he says it would be honest. Cervantes landed in March with the counsel to Sancho.

entries.quote: Yet such is oft the course of deeds that move the wheels of the world: small hands do them because they must, while the eyes of the great are elsewhere.
entries.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapter 2, The Council of Elrond (Elrond) (George Allen and Unwin, 1954), p. 283
entries.note: Verified on p. 283 of the 1954 Allen and Unwin text by search-inside; the opening word Yet was outside the snippet and rests on secondary witnesses. Add p. 283 to the source. A service line. Mind the Tolkien count: the carry holds several.

entries.quote: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze and loftier than the Pyramids’ royal pile, one that no wasting rain, no furious north wind can destroy, or the countless chain of years and the ages’ flight.
entries.source: Horace, Odes, Book III, ode 30, lines 1 to 5 (trans. C. E. Bennett, Loeb Classical Library, 1914)
entries.note: Verified in Bennett’s 1914 Loeb, p. 279, unchanged by the 1927 revision. Horace landed in March with the Epistle to Lollius. The work that outlasts its maker: November.

entries.quote: And we should consider every day lost on which we have not danced at least once.
entries.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Third Part, On Old and New Tablets, 23 (Zarathustra) (trans. Walter Kaufmann, 1954)
entries.note: Verified in Kaufmann, The Portable Nietzsche, p. 322. The source here puts the speaker before the translation, as the landed precedents do. Nietzsche stands at two of three after March.

entries.quote: I can resist everything except temptation.
entries.source: Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere’s Fan, First Act (Lord Darlington)
entries.note: Verified, First Act. It pulls against Discipline and Habit and the play rebukes it in the next line; wit by inversion, for the month of aphorisms if anywhere.

entries.quote: You can’t get away from yourself by moving from one place to another.
entries.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book I, chapter 2 (Jake Barnes)
entries.note: Verified, Book I, chapter 2, Jake to Robert Cohn. The alternate to 03-cfl-04: one Hemingway per month.

entries.quote: But then I have always supposed it to be my own fault—because I would not take the trouble of practising.
entries.source: Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice, ch. 31: vol. II, ch. 8 in the 1813 edition (Elizabeth Bennet, to Mr Darcy)
entries.note: Verified against the 1813 first edition text, dash included. On practice, but not the sentence the novel is known by; the fame test is its weak leg. Austen stands at one of three.

entries.quote: Just as iron rusts unless it is used, and water putrifies or, in cold, turns to ice, so our intellect spoils unless it is kept in use.
entries.source: Leonardo da Vinci, Notebooks, no. 1177 (The Literary Works of Leonardo da Vinci, ed. J. P. Richter, trans. mainly Mrs R. C. Bell, 1883)
entries.note: Verified in the 1883 Richter scans. The spelling putrifies is the 1883 edition’s own and a card needs a note saying so, which a VERIFIED line cannot carry: have a verifier rule it CORRECTED with that note before it lands. Richter files it under Philosophical Maxims, so Philosophy is as fair a tag as Diary.

entries.quote: But I maintain that she would come if we worked for her, and that so to work, even in poverty and obscurity, is worth while.
entries.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, chapter 6, the closing sentence (1929)
entries.note: CORRECTED: a note names her. She is Shakespeare’s sister, the gifted poet Woolf imagines, who died young and never wrote a word. The closing sentence of the book, so December’s by right.

entries.quote: For to be possessed of a vigorous mind is not enough; the prime requisite is rightly to apply it.
entries.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part I, first paragraph (trans. John Veitch, 1850)
entries.note: Verified in Veitch; the 1850 date is from memory, not from a scan. Right application of the mind: a clarity line.

entries.quote: The glorious masterpiece of man is to live to purpose; all other things: to reign, to lay up treasure, to build, are but little appendices and props.
entries.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book III, ch. 13, Of Experience (trans. Charles Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, Navarre Society, 1923)
entries.note: CORRECTED: the wording is Hazlitt’s later revision of Cotton as printed by the Navarre Society, 1923, vol. 5, p. 317; the 1877 Reeves and Turner text reads The great and glorious masterpiece of man is to know how to live to purpose. Ship with that note.

entries.quote: It is not enough to know, we must also apply; it is not enough to will, we must also do.
entries.source: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Maxims and Reflections, Life and Character, VI, no. 324 (trans. T. Bailey Saunders, 1893)
entries.note: Verified in the 1893 Macmillan first edition, maxim 324. Goethe landed in March with Faust’s last speech. A maxim for the month of maxims.

entries.quote: And in fact I did cut it in punishment for such stupidity: for there seemed to me no cause for a head to be adorned with hair and naked of learning—which was the more desired embellishment.
entries.source: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Response to Sor Filotea (1691), in Poems, Protest, and a Dream, p. 15 (trans. Margaret Sayers Peden, 1997)
entries.note: CORRECTED, confidence medium: Peden’s wording, but these words close a longer sentence, so the opening capital is the card’s; p. 15 rests on one secondary citation. Peden titles the work Response to the Most Illustrious Poetess Sor Filotea de la Cruz: the source should read Response to Sor Filotea. The it has no antecedent until hair arrives.

entries.quote: Refrain tonight, / And that shall lend a kind of easiness / To the next abstinence, the next more easy; / For use almost can change the stamp of nature.
entries.source: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 3, scene 4, lines 186 to 189, Folger edition (Hamlet)
entries.note: Verified in the Folger text, 3.4.186 to 189; Folger prints no stop after nature, so the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause. Held on the cap, not on merit: Shakespeare stands at two of three and this would be his last line of the year with nine months to come. Counsel from one character to another: May.

entries.quote: I know now, I understand at last, Constantine, that for us, whether we write or act, it is not the honour and glory of which I have dreamt that is important, it is the strength to endure.
entries.source: Anton Chekhov, The Sea-Gull, Act IV, to Treplieff (Nina) (trans. Marian Fell, 1912)
entries.note: CORRECTED: the locator is Act IV, to Treplieff, not her last speech; she speaks twice more. Wording is Fell’s, p. 220 of the 1912 Scribner volume. Chekhov landed in March with the letter to Nikolay and stands at two of three. The strength to endure: July.

entries.quote: But he that dares not grasp the thorn / Should never crave the rose.
entries.source: Anne Brontë, The Narrow Way (1848), lines 15 to 16, in The Complete Poems of Anne Brontë (ed. Clement Shorter, 1920), p. 145
entries.note: Verified in Shorter’s 1920 Complete Poems, p. 145: he that, not he who. Add the page to the source. Held to keep March under the cap for lines originally in English.

entries.quote: Climb Mount Fuji, / O snail, / but slowly, slowly.
entries.source: Kobayashi Issa, ‘Climb Mount Fuji’, in The Essential Haiku: Versions of Bashō, Buson, and Issa (trans. Robert Hass, 1994)
entries.note: Verified second hand, confidence medium: the Ecco page was not seen and the punctuation rests on a faithful reprint of Hass. Open the book before landing. Issa stands at one of three.

entries.quote: I’ve learned to live simply, wisely, / To look at the sky and pray to God, / And to take long walks before evening / To wear out this useless anxiety.
entries.source: Anna Akhmatova, ‘I’ve learned to live simply, wisely’ (1912), Rosary (1914), lines 1 to 4 (trans. Judith Hemschemeyer, 1990)
entries.note: Verified on several independent reprints credited to Hemschemeyer, confidence medium: the Zephyr volume was not opened and no page is cited. Tidier source: Rosary (1914). A quiet daily practice: October.

entries.quote: Yes, there is goal and meaning in our path - / but it’s the way that is the labour’s worth.
entries.source: Karin Boye, In Motion, The Hearths (1927), lines 3 to 4 (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
entries.note: Verified on the Karin Boye Society page, credited to McDuff’s Complete Poems (Bloodaxe, 1994). The spaced hyphen after path is the web setting; check the printed page for the mark before landing. The way is the labour’s worth: April’s own line.

entries.quote: The pitcher cries for water to carry / and a person for work that is real.
entries.source: Marge Piercy, To be of use, Circles on the Water (1982), closing lines; first in To Be of Use (1973)
entries.note: Verified against the Poetry Foundation text, credited to Circles on the Water (1982); nobody has seen the 1973 page. Honest source: Marge Piercy, To be of use, Circles on the Water (1982), closing lines; first in To Be of Use (1973). To be of use is September’s theme.

entries.quote: Live not for battles won. / Live not for the-end-of-the-song. / Live in the along.
entries.source: Gwendolyn Brooks, Speech to the Young: Speech to the Progress-Toward, Blacks (1991), closing lines; first in Family Pictures (1970)
entries.note: Verified against Blacks (1991), not the 1970 Family Pictures page. Honest source: Gwendolyn Brooks, Speech to the Young: Speech to the Progress-Toward, Blacks (1991), closing lines; first in Family Pictures (1970). Brooks stands at one of three. Live in the along: the Way.

entries.quote: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
entries.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part V, Proposition 42, Scholium, the closing sentence (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
entries.note: Verified closing line of the Ethics in Elwes. Carried to March as a discipline line and not used: it merely fits there, and as a closing sentence it belongs to December.

entries.quote: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
entries.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, ch. 4, answering Rousseau
entries.note: Verified in the 1792 text, immediately after the Rousseau quotation. Carried to March and not used, to hold the count of lines originally in English; power over themselves is also what September means by justice.
